title: Pancit Canton
description: The chewy, savoury-sweet egg noodle version of Filipino Pancit. Richer than Bihon thanks to oyster sauce and Chinese sausage, with a satisfying bite from thick wheat noodles.

method.instruction: Heat oil in a large wok over medium-high heat. Sauté garlic and onion until fragrant.
Add pork slices and Chinese sausage. Cook until the pork is browned and the sausage begins to render its fat. Add prawns and cook until just pink, then remove all meat and set aside.
Add carrot, sugar snap peas, and red capsicum to the wok. Stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until just tender, then remove and set aside.

Pour chicken stock, soy sauce, and oyster sauce into the wok and bring to a boil. Add the dry Canton noodles directly into the boiling broth — do not pre-soak. Toss and stir-fry until the noodles soften and absorb most of the liquid.
Return the meat and vegetables to the wok. Add shredded cabbage last and toss everything together until well combined and heated through.
Season with ground black pepper to taste. Transfer to a serving dish, top with chopped spring onion, and serve with calamansi or lemon wedges on the side.

notes.title: No Soaking Required
notes.content: Unlike Bihon, dry Canton noodles go straight into the boiling broth. They soften quickly through stir-frying and will turn mushy if pre-soaked.

notes.title: Sausage Fat
notes.content: Chinese sausage renders a naturally sweet fat as it cooks. Let it render before adding other ingredients — it adds significant flavour to the base.

notes.title: Mixed Pancit
notes.content: Combining half Bihon and half Canton noodles in one dish is popular and gives a great contrast of textures. Avoid cutting the noodles before serving — pancit symbolises long life.
